paragraphs: “Not the faintest idea, madam. Ah, madam, not the faintest!” cried Mitya, in nervous impatience, actually jumping up from his seat. “I’m begging you, madam, just listen to me. Give me two minutes to speak freely, so I can explain everything, the whole plan I’ve come with. Besides, I’m short of time. I’m in a terrible hurry,” Mitya cried hysterically. He felt she was about to start talking again and hoped to cut her off. “I’ve come in despair ... in the last gasp of despair, to beg you to lend me three thousand. A loan, but on safe security, madam, the safest, with the most trustworthy guarantees! Only let me explain—”

“You can tell me all that afterwards, afterwards!” Madame Hohlakov raised her hand and demanded silence in her turn. “And whatever you tell me, I know it all beforehand. I’ve told you so already. You ask for a certain sum, three thousand, but I can give you more, immeasurably more. I will save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you must listen to me.”
Mitya jumped up from his seat again.
“Madam, will you really be so kind!” he cried, deeply moved. “Good God, you’ve saved me! You’ve saved a man from a violent death, from a bullet.... My eternal gratitude—”
“I will give you more, infinitely more than three thousand!” cried Madame Hohlakov, looking with a radiant smile at Mitya’s delight.
“Infinitely? But I don’t need so much. I only need that fatal three thousand, and for my part I can give security for that sum, with infinite gratitude, and I propose a plan which—”

“Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it’s said and done.” Madame Hohlakov cut him short, with the modest triumph of a woman doing good. “I have promised to save you, and I will save you. I will save you as I saved Belmesov. What do you think of the gold-mines, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
“The gold-mines, madam? I’ve never thought anything about them.”

“But I have thought about them, for you. Over and over again. I’ve been watching you for the last month. A hundred times I’ve watched you walk past, and said to myself: there goes a man of energy who ought to be at the gold-mines. I’ve studied your gait and come to the conclusion: that is a man who would find gold.”
“From my gait, madam?” said Mitya, smiling.

“Yes, from your gait. Surely you don’t deny that you can tell character from the gait, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Science supports it. I’m all for science and realism now. After all this business with Father Zossima, which has upset me so much, from this very day I’m a realist and I want to devote myself to practical usefulness. I’m cured. ‘Enough!’ as Turgenev says.”
“But, madam, the three thousand you so generously promised to lend me—”

“It’s yours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov cut in at once. “The money is as good as in your pocket. Not three thousand, but three million, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, in no time at all. I make you a present of the idea: you will find gold-mines, make millions, come back and become a leading man, and wake us up and lead us to better things. Are we to leave everything to the Jews? You will found institutions and enterprises of all sorts. You will help the poor, and they will bless you. This is the age of railways, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You’ll become famous and indispensable to the Department of Finance, which is so badly off at present. The falling value of the rouble keeps me awake at night, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. People don’t know that side of me—”

“Madam, madam!” Dmitri interrupted, with an uneasy foreboding. “I may well follow your advice, your wise advice, madam.... I may go ... to the gold-mines.... I’ll come and see you again about it ... many times, in fact ... but now, that three thousand you so generously ... oh, that would set me free, and if you could today ... you see, I haven’t a minute, not a minute to lose today—”
“Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, enough!” Madame Hohlakov interrupted emphatically. “The question is, will you go to the gold-mines or not? Have you made up your mind completely? Answer yes or no.”
“I’ll go, madam, afterwards.... I’ll go wherever you like ... but now—”
“Wait!” cried Madame Hohlakov. She jumped up and ran to a handsome bureau with a great many little drawers, and began pulling out one drawer after another, searching for something in desperate haste.

“The three thousand,” thought Mitya, his heart almost stopping, “and on the spot ... with no papers or formalities ... that’s what I call doing things like a gentleman! She’s a splendid woman, if only she didn’t talk so much!”
“Here!” cried Madame Hohlakov, running joyfully back to Mitya. “Here’s what I was looking for!”
It was a tiny silver ikon on a cord, the kind sometimes worn next to the skin with a cross.

“This is from Kiev, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” she went on reverently, “from the relics of the Holy Martyr Varvara. Let me put it round your neck myself, and with it dedicate you to a new life, to a new career.”

And she actually put the cord round his neck and began arranging it. In extreme embarrassment, Mitya bent down and helped her, and at last he got it under his necktie and collar, through his shirt, to his chest.
“Now you can set off,” Madame Hohlakov pronounced, sitting down triumphantly in her place again.

“Madam, I’m so touched. I really don’t know how to thank you ... for such kindness, but ... If only you knew how precious time is to me.... That sum of money, for which I’ll be indebted to your generosity.... Oh, madam, since you are so kind to me, so touchingly generous,” Mitya exclaimed impulsively, “then let me tell you ... though of course you’ve known it a long time ... that I love someone here.... I have been unfaithful to Katya ... Katerina Ivanovna, I should say.... Oh, I’ve behaved inhumanly, dishonorably toward her, but I fell in love here with another woman ... a woman you, madam, perhaps despise, since you know everything already, but whom I cannot leave on any account, and so that three thousand now—”

“Leave everything, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov interrupted in the most decisive tone. “Leave everything, especially women. Gold-mines are your goal, and there’s no place for women there. Afterwards, when you come back rich and famous, you’ll find the girl of your heart in the highest society. She will be a modern girl, a girl of education and advanced ideas. By that time the woman question, which is only dawning now, will have gained ground, and the new woman will have appeared.”
“Madam, that’s not the point, not at all....” Mitya clasped his hands in entreaty.

“Yes, it is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it’s just what you need, the very thing you’re longing for, though you don’t realize it yourself. I’m not at all opposed to the present women’s movement, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The development of women, and even the political emancipation of women in the near future, that’s my ideal. I have a daughter myself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. People don’t know that side of me. I wrote a letter to the author Shtchedrin on that subject. He has taught me so much, so much about the vocation of woman. So last year I sent him an anonymous letter of two lines: ‘I kiss and embrace you, my teacher, for the modern woman. Persevere.’ And I signed it ‘A Mother.’ I thought of signing it ‘A contemporary Mother,’ and hesitated, but I kept to the simple ‘Mother.’ There’s more moral beauty in that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. And the word ‘contemporary’ might have reminded him of ‘_The Contemporary_,’ a painful memory for him because of the censorship.... Good heavens, what’s the matter!”
“Madam!” cried Mitya, jumping up at last and clasping his hands before her in helpless entreaty. “You’ll make me weep if you put off what you have so generously—”

“Oh, do weep, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, do weep! That’s a noble feeling ... such a path lies open before you! Tears will ease your heart, and later you’ll come back rejoicing. You’ll hurry to me from Siberia on purpose to share your joy with me—”
“But let me speak too!” Mitya cried suddenly. “For the last time I beg you, tell me, can I have the sum you promised me today? If not, when may I come for it?”
“What sum, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
“The three thousand you promised me ... that you so generously—”
“Three thousand? Roubles? Oh, no, I haven’t got three thousand,” Madame Hohlakov announced with serene surprise. Mitya was stunned.
“But you said just now ... you said ... you said it was as good as in my hands—”

“Oh, no, you misunderstood me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. In that case you misunderstood me. I was talking about the gold-mines. It’s true I promised you more, infinitely more than three thousand, I remember it all now, but I meant the gold-mines.”
“But the money? The three thousand?” Mitya exclaimed, awkwardly.

“Oh, if you meant money, I haven’t any. I haven’t a penny, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m quarreling with my steward about it, and I’ve just borrowed five hundred roubles from Miüsov myself. No, no, I have no money. And do you know, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, if I had, I wouldn’t give it to you. In the first place, I never lend money. Lending money means losing friends. And I especially wouldn’t give it to you. I wouldn’t give it to you because I like you and want to save you, because all you need is the gold-mines, the gold-mines, the gold-mines!”
“Oh, the devil!” roared Mitya, and he brought his fist down on the table with all his might.
“Aie! Aie!” cried Madame Hohlakov, alarmed, and she flew to the other end of the drawing-room.

Mitya spat on the floor and strode rapidly out of the room, out of the house, into the street, into the darkness! He walked like a man possessed, beating himself on the breast, on the very spot where he had struck himself two days before, in front of Alyosha, the last time he saw him, in the dark, on the road. What those blows on his breast meant, _on that spot_, and what he intended by them, was for the time being a secret. No one in the world knew it, and he had not told even Alyosha. But for him that secret meant more than disgrace; it meant ruin, suicide. He had made up his mind to that if he did not get the three thousand to pay his debt to Katerina Ivanovna, and so remove from his breast, from _that spot on his breast_, the shame he carried there, which weighed on his conscience. All this will be fully explained to the reader later. But now that his last hope had vanished, this man, so strong in appearance, burst out crying like a little child a few steps from the Hohlakovs’ house. He walked on, not knowing what he was doing, and wiped away his tears with his fist. In this way he reached the square, and suddenly realized he had stumbled against something. He heard a piercing wail from an old woman whom he had almost knocked down.
“Good Lord, you’ve nearly killed me! Why don’t you look where you’re going, you good-for-nothing?”
“Why, it’s you!” cried Mitya, recognizing the old woman in the dark. It was the old servant who waited on Samsonov, whom Mitya had particularly noticed the day before.
“And who are you, my good sir?” said the old woman, in quite a different voice. “I can’t make you out in the dark.”
“You live at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. You’re the servant there?”
“That’s right, sir. I was just running out to Prohoritch’s.... But I don’t know you now.”
“Tell me, my good woman, is Agrafena Alexandrovna there now?” said Mitya, beside himself with suspense. “I took her to the house myself some time ago.”
“She was there, sir. She stayed a little while and went off again.”
“What? Went away?” cried Mitya. “When did she go?”
“Why, as soon as she came. She only stayed a minute. She just told Kuzma Kuzmitch a tale that made him laugh, and then she ran away.”
“You’re lying, damn you!” roared Mitya.
“Aie! Aie!” shrieked the old woman, but Mitya had vanished.
He ran with all his might to the house where Grushenka lived. At the moment he reached it, Grushenka was on her way to Mokroe. It was no more than a quarter of an hour since she had left.
Fenya was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother, the old cook Matryona, when “the captain” ran in. Fenya let out a piercing shriek at the sight of him.
“You scream?” roared Mitya. “Where is she?”
But before the terrified Fenya could say a word, he fell in a heap at her feet.
“Fenya, for Christ’s sake, tell me, where is she?”
“I don’t know. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear, I don’t know. You can kill me, but I can’t tell you.” Fenya swore and protested. “You went out with her yourself not long ago—”
“She came back!”
“Indeed she didn’t. I swear to God she didn’t come back.”
“You’re lying!” shouted Mitya. “I can tell where she is from how scared you are.”

He rushed away. Fenya, in her fright, was glad she had got off so easily. But she knew very well it was only because he was in such a hurry; otherwise she might not have fared so well. But as he ran, he surprised both Fenya and old Matryona by an unexpected action. On the table stood a brass mortar with a pestle in it, a small brass pestle not much more than six inches long. Mitya had already opened the door with one hand when, with the other, he snatched up the pestle and thrust it into his side pocket.
“Oh, Lord! He’s going to murder somebody!” cried Fenya, flinging up her hands.
